title: Green Sahara corridors open across Africa and Arabia

facts.text: The exceptionally intense Eemian humid period greened northern Africa, more strongly than the Holocene's African humid period.
It opened pathways for early humans to cross Arabia and northern Africa.
Modern humans dispersed via North Africa and the Arabian Peninsula about 130,000 to 115,000 years ago at least.
The Red Sea coastal route was extremely arid before 140,000 and after 115,000 years ago.
Such humid phases come with interglacials and precession minima, while glacial stages bring dry periods.

facts.text: The Last Interglacial followed the Penultimate Glacial Period and lasted until about 115,000 years ago; it corresponds to Marine Isotope Stage 5e.
It was one of the warmest spells of the last 800,000 years, up to about 2 °C warmer than the Holocene, with CO2 near 280 ppm.
Warmth peaked about 128,000–123,000 years ago; around 125,000 years ago forests grew at North Cape, Norway, today tundra.
Arctic summers ran about 2–4 °C warmer than in 2011; abrupt cold spells around 120,000 years ago followed shifts in the North Atlantic Current.
The end of the Riss (Penultimate) glaciation and start of this interglacial is the proposed beginning of the Late Pleistocene.

title: Eemian sea-level highstand as West Antarctic ice melts

facts.text: At its peak, sea level stood probably 6–9 m above today's, with Greenland, thermal expansion and Antarctica all contributing.
The West Antarctic Ice Sheet appears to have collapsed around 125,000 years ago, when temperatures resembled the early 21st century's.
Seas may have risen as fast as 2.5 m per century; East Antarctica's Wilkes Basin lost ice worth about 0.5 m.
High seas made Fennoscandia and Jutland islands and flooded much of northwestern Europe and the West Siberian Plain.
Fossil coral reefs from this highstand, now stranded above sea level, are common in the Caribbean and along the Red Sea.

title: Klasies River: early modern humans on the South African coast

facts.text: Excavations at Klasies River Caves found Middle Stone Age human habitation beginning about 125,000 years ago.
Being close to the coast and grasslands, the caves' inhabitants exploited both marine life and land animals.
Human remains include finger bones 90,000–100,000 years old and jaws about 119,000 years old.
Stone tools at Jebel Faya (Faya-1) in the United Arab Emirates show modern humans in Arabia at least 125,000 years ago.
Groups may have left Africa by two routes: the Nile, Sinai and Levant, and across the Bab-el-Mandeb strait when seas were low.
Tools on a raised 125,000-year-old reef at Abdur, Eritrea, suggest coastal foragers ate shellfish over 100,000 years ago.
These early migrations do not seem to have led to lasting colonisation and had receded by about 80,000 years ago.

title: Long-horned bison evolve in North America

facts.text: At the start of the Last Interglacial, about 130,000 years ago, steppe bison spread from Alaska into central North America as the Laurentide ice melted.
There they gave rise to the giant long-horned bison, Bison latifrons, first known from Colorado's Snowmass site about 120,000 years ago.
By 60,000 years ago long-horned bison had given rise to Bison antiquus, widely considered the ancestor of the modern American bison.
At Neumark-Nord in Germany, remains of at least 57 straight-tusked elephants date to the Last Interglacial, about 120,000 years ago.
Systematic butchery there and at Lehringen, Taubach and Gröbern points to widespread Neanderthal hunting of these elephants in Eemian Germany.
Neanderthals at Neumark-Nord hunted elephants regularly, perhaps every 5 to 6 years, and may have rendered fat from their bones.

It long predates modern humans, who reached the region roughly 55,000–50,000 years ago, and left no living descendants.

facts.text: Dansgaard–Oeschger events, rapid climate fluctuations, occurred 25 times during the Last Glacial Period.
They are best recorded in Greenland ice cores, which reach back to the end of the Eemian, about 115,000 years ago.
In sharp cases Greenland warmed about 8 °C within 40 years; a 5 °C rise over 30–40 years was more typical.
They arose when ice volume and CO2 were intermediate, a window in which the Atlantic overturning circulation was bistable.
Each nudged CO2 up about 5 ppm and weakened the Indonesian–Australian monsoon; a 1,470-year rhythm is proposed but debated.
Acheulean tools vanish from the archaeological record around 100,000 years ago.
More complex Middle Paleolithic tool kits, such as the Mousterian and Aterian industries, replaced them.
The Mousterian displaced it in Europe and the Middle East by around 125,000 years ago, but it may have lasted until about 50,000 years ago in East Asia.

title: Heinrich events: iceberg armadas in the North Atlantic

facts.text: In Heinrich events, great fleets of icebergs broke from the Laurentide ice sheet and drifted through Hudson Strait into the North Atlantic.
They are especially well documented for the Wisconsin glaciation, about 75,000 to 11,000 years ago.
Melting icebergs dropped rock debris as Heinrich layers and poured fresh water into the North Atlantic, likely altering ocean circulation.
Iceberg discharges between 21,000 and 11,500 years ago coincided with subtropical droughts.
Why the ice sheet became unstable is still debated.

title: Mastodons and giant beavers vanish from the far north

facts.text: American mastodons, which had lived in North America's far north in Last Interglacial forests, were extirpated there about 75,000 years ago as the Wisconsin glaciation (MIS 4) set in.
This happened long before people arrived, and confined mastodons to lands south of the North American ice sheets.
Giant beavers likewise vanished from Alaska and the Yukon after 75,000 years ago as conditions grew more hostile.

title: Toba supereruption

facts.text: Toba in Sumatra erupted around 74,000 years ago, a VEI 8 supereruption and one of the largest known in the Cenozoic.
It released about 2,800 km3 of magma, left the caldera now filled by Lake Toba, and covered India in about 5 cm of ash.
It struck during the rapid cooling into MIS 4; whether it sped that cooling is debated, and Arabian Sea records suggest not.
The Toba catastrophe theory ties it to a human population bottleneck, but that causal link remains highly controversial.
Eruptions of this size happen somewhere on Earth every 50,000 to 100,000 years.

title: Late Pleistocene megafauna extinctions begin

facts.text: From around 50,000 years ago most large land animals outside Africa died out, an extinction unprecedented for its bias toward large species.

Hunting, climate change or both are blamed; the balance is long debated, though most scholars accept some human role.
Africa was affected less than other continents; mammal diversity lost since could take 5–7 million years to recover.

Ice up to 3 km thick covered much of northern Europe, Asia, North America, Greenland and Antarctica.

title: Missoula floods scour the Channeled Scablands

facts.text: Glacial Lake Missoula, dammed by ice on the Clark Fork River, held up to about 2,500 km³ of water.
The dam failed and re-formed repeatedly, unleashing dozens of floods, about one every 55 years, between 15,000 and 13,000 years ago.
The largest discharged about 10 km³ an hour, sweeping across eastern Washington and into Oregon's Willamette Valley.
Together the floods stripped about 210 km³ of loess, sediment and basalt from the Channeled Scablands.

facts.text: Near the end of the last glaciation, Altai glaciers dammed the Chuya River, forming a large lake in the Chuya and Kurai basins.
According to some geomorphologists, the lake, holding up to 600 km³, burst in cataclysmic floods down the Katun River.
The floods left giant current ripples up to 18 m high.

facts.text: The Magdalenian reindeer hunters, 21,000–13,000 years ago, descended mainly from Gravettian groups who had retreated to southwestern Europe during the Last Glacial Maximum.
Around 15,000 years ago, after the harsh Oldest Dryas, they moved north to recolonise northern Europe, reaching Britain and, eastward, Poland.
From about 14,000 years ago Epigravettian-linked Western Hunter-Gatherers spread north across the Alps, largely replacing them.

title: Cave lion dies out

facts.text: Cave lions died out almost simultaneously across their range about 15,000–14,000 years ago, lingering roughly 1,000 years longer in North America.
A population bottleneck between 47,000 and 18,000 years ago, probably driven partly by climatic instability, had already cut their genetic diversity.
The cause is unknown; climate change, shrinking prey and competition with other carnivores and humans have all been suggested.

contested_note: The cause of the cave lion's extinction is unknown, part of the long-running debate over the causes of the Late Pleistocene megafauna extinctions.

facts.text: While the north warmed, the Southern Hemisphere south of 40°S underwent intense atmospheric and oceanic cooling between 14,700 and 13,000 years ago.
Temperatures fell, atmospheric CO2 stopped rising and glaciers readvanced, as in New Zealand's Southern Alps; Tasmania records a matching cold spell.
It is thought to have been caused by a meltwater pulse, probably from the Antarctic or Laurentide ice sheet.
It may have pushed the southern polar front north and increased precipitation in the Andes.
After about 13,000 years ago warming resumed and glaciers withdrew abruptly from the moraines they had built.

facts.text: The Bølling–Allerød interstadial, about 14,690 to 12,890 years ago, opened with abrupt warming in the Northern Hemisphere.
Greenland's NorthGRIP ice core records its onset at 14,600 years ago, and atmospheric methane rose about 14,700 years ago.
A stronger Atlantic overturning circulation carried heat north while the Southern Hemisphere cooled, a 'polar seesaw'.
The Allerød phase lifted northern Atlantic temperatures almost to present-day levels.
The warmth let people repopulate Eurasia from glacial refuges; in Beringia shrub tundra replaced dry steppe after 14,000 years ago.

facts.text: Global sea level rose 16–25 m in about 400–500 years, at roughly 40–60 mm a year.
These are the fastest known rates of post-glacial sea-level rise, attributed to the rapid collapse of continental ice sheets.
The pulse began with, or just after, the abrupt Bølling–Allerød warming recorded in Greenland ice.
The West Antarctic ice sheet shrank between 15,000 and 14,000 years ago, matching an abrupt sea-level rise around 14,500 years ago.
It is the most widely recognised and least disputed of the named meltwater pulses.

facts.text: North Africa turned wetter about 14,600–14,500 years ago, as Heinrich event 1 ended and the Bølling–Allerød warming began.

Lake Victoria, dry around 15,000 years ago, refilled and overflowed, and Lakes Albert and Tana spilled into the White and Blue Nile.
The Nile took its current form about 15,000 years ago.
Lakes such as Lake Chad formed or grew, glaciers grew on Kilimanjaro, and the Sahara shrank.

title: Natufian foragers settle in the Levant

facts.text: The Natufian culture of the Levant, radiocarbon-dated to 12,500–9,500 BC, supported sedentary or semi-sedentary communities before agriculture.
Its settlements were larger and more permanent than earlier ones, some with round stone buildings, as at Ain Mallaha, and the first evidence of food storage.
Natufians harvested wild cereals and hunted gazelles; the cold, dry Younger Dryas pushed early settled groups back toward a more mobile life.

title: Paisley Caves: pre-Clovis people in Oregon

facts.text: Human coprolites from Oregon's Paisley Caves, radiocarbon dated to about 14,300–14,400 years ago, hold the oldest human DNA found in North America.
The DNA ties these pre-Clovis people to Siberia or Asia; they ate plants, seeds, rodents, fish and insects.
Critics question whether the coprolites are human and whether their dates hold, suspecting contamination by leached human DNA.

title: Great Lakes basins begin to fill

facts.text: The Great Lakes began forming around 14,000 years ago, as retreating ice sheets exposed the basins they had carved and meltwater filled them.
In Wisconsin the ice also began to retreat about 14,000 years ago as the climate warmed.
The Older Dryas was a brief cold stadial between the Bølling and Allerød warm phases, about 14,000 years ago.
Its dates vary by about 400 years between methods, but it lasted only a century or two.
Ice readvanced in places, as in the Littleton–Bethlehem readvance and Canada's Shulie Lake phase.

title: Megafauna die out across the Americas

facts.text: North American extinctions clustered around 13,800–11,400 years ago, with the Younger Dryas onset and Clovis; across the Americas they spanned 3,000 years at most.
About 72% of North American and 83% of South American megafaunal species died out, including every mammal over 1,000 kg.
Ground sloths, litopterns and the last notoungulates vanished from the mainland around 12,000 years ago, with most other large mammals.
Losing the American megafauna is estimated to have cut methane production by about 9.6 million tons a year.
Butchered bones, such as an Ohio ground sloth dated 13,738–13,435 BP, show people hunted megafauna, but the causes remain debated.

contested_note: Whether human hunting, climate change or both caused the extinctions is a long-running controversy, though most scholars accept at least a contributory human role.

facts.text: By 21,000 BP the Cordilleran and Laurentide ice sheets had merged east of the Rocky Mountains, closing a route into North America's interior.
A gap between them opened about 13,800 ± 500 years ago by 2022 estimates; older studies put it at 13,000–12,000 BP.
That is later than the earliest widely accepted archaeological sites, so the corridor could not have carried the first people south.

title: Clovis culture spreads across North America

facts.text: The Clovis culture spanned about 13,050–12,750 years ago; its type site, Blackwater Draw in New Mexico, held tools alongside Columbian mammoth remains.
Its hallmark was the fluted Clovis point, a large lanceolate projectile point also used for cutting.
Mobile hunter-gatherers, Clovis people relied on big game, especially mammoths, and may have contributed to megafauna extinctions, a controversial idea.
A 2022 study found the ice-free corridor impassable until about 13,800 years ago, long after people had reached lands south of the ice.
From about 12,750–12,600 years ago Clovis gave way to regional cultures such as Folsom.

facts.text: A VEI 6 Plinian eruption, comparable to Pinatubo in 1991, expelled about 6 km³ of magma and left the Laacher See crater lake in western Germany.
Its tephra dammed the Rhine into a 140 km² lake; when the dam broke, an outburst flood left deposits as far as Bonn.
Dated to 13,006 ± 9 calibrated years ago, it preceded the Younger Dryas by over a century, though 1990s research had proposed it as a trigger.

facts.text: Fed by meltwater from the retreating Laurentide Ice Sheet, Lake Agassiz spread over parts of Manitoba, Ontario, Minnesota, North Dakota and Saskatchewan around 13,000 years ago.
At its greatest extent it may have covered 440,000 km², more than any lake today and about the area of the Black Sea.
From about 13,500 BP it overflowed south through Glacial River Warren toward the Mississippi; at times it drained east to Lake Superior or northwest to the Arctic.
A drainage about 13,000 years ago may have caused the Younger Dryas, long the most supported explanation for that cold spell.
Its huge freshwater releases are thought to have disrupted ocean circulation and affected climate and sea level.

title: Champlain Sea floods the St. Lawrence lowlands

facts.text: Land still pressed down by ice let rising seas flood the St. Lawrence and Ottawa valleys, forming the Champlain Sea from about 13,000 years ago.
About 12,000 years ago the ice dam holding Lake Vermont failed, dropping the lake 91 m within hours or days before salt water swept in.
The sea shrank steadily as the land rebounded, lasting until about 10,000 years ago.
Hunter-gatherers first reached Cyprus around 11,000–10,000 BC; the Aetokremnos site may record hunting of dwarf hippos and dwarf elephants.
They introduced wild boar to the island around 12,000 years ago.
Cyprus's dwarf elephant and pygmy hippopotamus later vanished, and the genet Genetta plesictoides died out after humans and invasive species arrived.

title: Irish elk briefly returns to northern Europe

facts.text: The Irish elk's range collapsed during the Last Glacial Maximum: few remains date between 27,500 and 14,600 years ago, and none between 23,300 and 17,500.
It recolonised northern Europe in the Bølling–Allerød; most Irish remains date to the Allerød, around 13,000 years ago.
Its range shrank again in the Younger Dryas, and it had vanished from northern Europe by that period's end.

title: Pygmy mammoths die out on the Channel Islands

facts.text: Columbian mammoths that reached California's Channel Islands evolved into the pygmy mammoth, under half mainland size, living there 80,000–13,000 years ago.
Their youngest records, about 13,000 years old, coincide with rising seas shrinking the islands, the first people there and declining conifer forests.
The people of Arlington Springs Man, on Santa Rosa Island, are thought to have hunted them.

title: Younger Dryas impact hypothesis

facts.text: A fringe hypothesis claims a comet or meteor impact or airburst about 12,900 years ago disrupted Atlantic circulation and set off the Younger Dryas.
Richard Firestone and colleagues introduced it in 2007, also blaming the impact for megafaunal extinctions.
Most relevant experts reject it for lack of clear evidence, and the Hiawatha crater, once linked to it, proved to be 58 million years old.

contested_note: A fringe hypothesis, widely rejected by most relevant experts; the Younger Dryas page calls an impact cause very unlikely.

facts.text: The Younger Dryas, about 12,900 to 11,700 years ago, was the last cold phase of the Last Glacial Period, a return to glacial conditions.
Annual temperatures fell about 3 °C in North America, 2–6 °C in Europe and up to 10 °C in Greenland, where cooling took 3 years or less.
Scientists agree a severe weakening of the Atlantic overturning circulation caused it; a Lake Agassiz meltwater flood or a volcanic trigger are proposed explanations.
The Southern Hemisphere warmed, drought hit the African humid period region, and Altiplano lakes reached a peak.
It ended as rapidly as it began, with dramatic warming over about 50 years that closed the Pleistocene.

title: Short-faced bear Arctodus dies out

facts.text: Arctodus simus, averaging about 625 kg and reaching 957 kg, was one of the largest land carnivorans ever and ranged across North America.
It vanished from Beringia about 23,000 years ago, during the Last Glacial Maximum, possibly from sharp cooling tied to Heinrich event 2.
Elsewhere it died out about 12,800 years ago; vegetation shifts that cut its food supply and competition with brown bears are suggested causes.

title: Last scimitar-toothed cats (Homotherium)

facts.text: Homotherium, a lion-sized scimitar-toothed cat of up to about 250 kg, had lived across North America, Eurasia and Africa for some 4 million years.
Its youngest well-dated remains, from southern Alberta, are about 12,715–12,655 years old; with Smilodon it was among the last machairodonts.
Its extinction, like Smilodon's, has been linked to the loss of the large prey it relied on, such as mammoths, bison and horses.

title: Last Columbian mammoths

facts.text: The Columbian mammoth, up to 4.2 m tall and 12.5 tonnes, ranged from southern Canada to Costa Rica and outsized the woolly mammoth.
Its latest calibrated date, from Colorado's Dent site, is 12,705–12,124 years ago, as the Younger Dryas began; no Holocene survival is recorded.
Clovis people hunted or scavenged it; its extinction is blamed on climate-driven habitat loss, human hunting, or both.

title: Macrauchenia, among the last litopterns, dies out

facts.text: Macrauchenia, a long-necked hoofed mammal, was one of the last members of the Litopterna, an order native to South America for over 60 million years.
It died out around 12,000 years ago with most large mammals of the Americas, after people reached South America at least 14,500 years ago.
At Paso Otero 5 in the Argentine Pampas its burned bones lie with Fishtail spear points among other extinct megafauna.
